power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "P ≥ 0.750", Text = "These exploratory comparisons detected no association (all P ≥ 0.750), but non-significance does not establish independence or exclude unmeasured acquisition confounding."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P ≥ 0.750", "P = 0.22"), Sentence = c("These exploratory comparisons detected no association (all P ≥ 0.750), but non-significance does not establish independence or exclude unmeasured acquisition confounding.", "The original image-level Wilcoxon comparison for EfficientNet-B0 did not detect a difference (P = 0.22); this does not establish equivalence to random attribution or absence of class-relevant information." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Objectives: To determine whether similar baseline discrimination conceals different responses to synthetic occlusion, whether loss of discrimination is accompanied by reduced confidence, and whether spatial attributions are reproducible in intraoral ultrasonography models.
Methods: We analysed 477 images from 40 healthy volunteers, using acquisition position to label superior and inferior subregions.
Five architectures were evaluated across five training seeds on a subject-independent test set of 97 images from eight volunteers.
Images underwent constant-intensity occlusion at boundaries spanning 30-70% of image depth and an area-matched band-occlusion control.
Attribution analyses assessed variation across seeds and class-activation methods and compared attribution-guided insertion with random insertion.
Results: Seed-mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.958 to 0.972, with rankings reversing across seeds.
EfficientNet-B0 fell below 0.60 in 49 of 50 boundary-sweep conditions, compared with zero to two for the other architectures; the difference persisted with area-matched masking.
Under 50% occlusion, its mean confidence on incorrect predictions rose to 0.989 and expected calibration error from 0.094 to 0.478.
Between two inference runs, EfficientNet-B0's per-seed occluded AUCs differed by up to 0.161; seed means were 0.51-0.55 in both.
Attribution patterns varied across seeds and methods.
Conclusions: Similar baseline discrimination concealed different occlusion responses, and loss of discrimination could coexist with high confidence.
Attribution reproducibility provided a further constraint on interpretation.
These findings concern the evaluated pipelines and synthetic masks; they do not establish anatomical mechanisms or clinical reliability.

Advances in knowledge: Joint evaluation of perturbation sensitivity, confidence under perturbation and attribution reproducibility distinguished model behaviours that baseline discrimination alone did not reveal in intraoral ultrasonography.
Intraoral ultrasonography provides real-time imaging without ionizing radiation.
It has been investigated for ultrasound-guided resection of buccal squamous cell carcinoma [1] and for preoperative measurement of tumour depth and surgical margins [2, 3].

text.text: Other applications include oral and maxillofacial assessment [4], mucosal characterization [5], salivary gland assessment [6] and imaging with dedicated intraoral probes [7].

text.text: Interpretation depends on probe placement and recognition of the imaged tissue layers.
Deep learning has been applied to dental implant planning in cone-beam computed tomography [8], periapical disease detection in dental radiographs [9] and ultrasound in other specialties [10, 11].

text.text: Its use in intraoral ultrasonography remains comparatively limited, motivating evaluation of model behaviour beyond classification performance.
The buccal mucosa is a useful setting for this methodological evaluation.
It provides tissue for buccinator musculomucosal flaps [12] and mucosal grafts [13].

text.text: Ultrasonographic descriptions of facial tissue layers provide a general anatomical framework for interpreting such images [14].

text.text: In the present study, the superior and inferior acquisition regions were defined by probe position relative to the underlying musculature (Section 2.2).
Differences in the imaged tissue layers motivated depth-oriented perturbations, without assuming that a particular tissue boundary was the only discriminative feature.
For models with similar classification performance, a practical question is whether they also behave similarly when image information is altered.
Baseline discrimination does not characterize dependence on image features or responses to altered inputs [15, 16].
text.formatted: Baseline discrimination does not characterize dependence on image features or responses to altered inputs <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>.

text.text: Confidence and visual attribution offer additional information, but their usefulness depends on how they behave when performance deteriorates and on whether the explanations are reproducible.
A Grad-CAM overlay [17] from one trained model may appear anatomically plausible without establishing either property [18] [19] [20] [21] [22].
text.formatted: A Grad-CAM overlay <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> from one trained model may appear anatomically plausible without establishing either property <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: This leaves a model-selection and interpretation problem beyond the established observation that accuracy alone is insufficient: performance, confidence and attribution may give different accounts of the same model.
We chose superior-inferior buccal subregion classification as a methodological test case.

Because the operator knows the probe position, the labels are fixed at acquisition and independent of retrospective image interpretation, and the expected anatomical differences motivate depth-oriented perturbations.

For the same reason, the task is not intended for immediate clinical use; it offers a controlled setting in which to establish evaluation practices that can be applied to future clinical intraoral ultrasound models.
The labels do not, however, identify which image features distinguish the classes or provide a pixel-level anatomical reference.
The task permits comparison of model responses to controlled image changes without treating those changes as definitive tests of anatomical understanding.

We evaluated five architectures spanning residual, dense and compound-scaled convolutional families, a modernized convolutional design (ConvNeXt-Tiny) and a vision transformer (DeiT-Tiny), each across five random seeds.

We asked whether similar baseline discrimination conceals different responses to partial image occlusion; whether deterioration in discrimination is accompanied by reduced confidence or instead by confident errors; and whether attribution patterns remain reproducible across training seeds and class-activation methods.
Boundary sweeps and an area-matched control examined the scope of the occlusion response, while comparison with random insertion assessed the support for attribution-based interpretation.
These questions concern the evaluated training pipelines and controlled perturbations, rather than intrinsic properties of architecture families or demonstrated clinical failure.

>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Discussion</head>

text.text: This study examined how models with similar baseline discrimination differed when evaluated through perturbation responses, confidence and spatial attribution.
Acquisition-position classification provided a tractable test case in intraoral ultrasonography without requiring a diagnostic claim.

Expert agreement supported the interpretability of selected acquisition-defined labels, but neither the labels nor expert reading supplied a complete reference for the image features a model should use.
The central finding was a mismatch between baseline performance and behaviour under altered inputs.
Five architectures achieved similar observed baseline discrimination, yet EfficientNet-B0 fell below AUC 0.60 in 49 of 50 boundary-sweep conditions and remained sensitive in the area-matched control.
Its loss of discrimination was accompanied by highly confident errors rather than reduced confidence.
Spatial attribution patterns also varied across seeds and methods, limiting their ability to resolve the interpretation of model behaviour.
The contribution is therefore the joint characterization of these discrepancies in intraoral ultrasonography, rather than a general assertion that accuracy alone is insufficient.
The experiments do not identify their anatomical or architectural mechanism.
Seed-mean AUC ranged from 0.958 to 0.972 and F1 from 0.888 to 0.911.
Pairwise rankings reversed across seeds, and the eight-subject test cohort leaves substantial uncertainty.
Non-significant exploratory comparisons cannot demonstrate equivalence.
Architecture choice based on a single run would not capture the observed variability or the differences under synthetic perturbation.
EfficientNet-B7 performed poorly in cross-validation before test evaluation.
Its larger capacity is one possible explanation, but overparameterization was not tested directly.
Differences between cross-validation and test rankings may also reflect the small subject counts in the folds (Section 4.7).
EfficientNet-B0 had a mid-range baseline AUC but the largest observed loss under the tested masks.
Boundary sweeps showed that the response was not confined to the primary 50% boundary, and the area-matched control showed that it persisted across mask positions when the removed area was fixed.
The resulting distinction between evaluated pipelines was largely absent from the baseline performance comparison.
This supports considering perturbation response as an additional dimension of model comparison, while retaining the uncertainty from the small test cohort and the differences in training settings.
It does not establish an intrinsic robustness ranking of architecture families.
Attribution maps do not by themselves establish causal use of the highlighted regions [42].
text.formatted: Attribution maps do not by themselves establish causal use of the highlighted regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>.

text.text: Constant-intensity occlusion changes both image content and the input distribution.
The retained AUC of four architectures under 50% occlusion shows discrimination under those masked inputs; the larger loss for EfficientNet-B0 shows sensitivity to the intervention.

Boundary and area controls extend this observation across specified locations and removal fractions, but do not separate dependence on distributed anatomical information from susceptibility to the artificial mask.
Potential explanations include different dependence on spatially distributed image information and different susceptibility to the artificial mask.

Residual propagation [24], depthwise-separable convolutions and squeezeand-excitation weighting [26] provide architectural context for generating hypotheses, but this experiment did not isolate their effects.
text.formatted: Residual propagation <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>, depthwise-separable convolutions and squeezeand-excitation weighting <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> provide architectural context for generating hypotheses, but this experiment did not isolate their effects.

text.text: Differences in tuning, optimization and execution also prevent attributing the observed response to a particular design component.
The most defensible interpretation is a difference among the evaluated model pipelines under the specified perturbations.
Class-wise responses were largely shared (Section 3.4).

The inverted default reported for DenseNet-121 in a single best-fold run lay at the extreme of the seed distribution, so we do not interpret it as a property of dense connectivity -an instance of the same single-run instability this study documents for attribution.
The confidence response gives the occlusion result a separate implication.
EfficientNet-B0 had the lowest mean confidence on incorrect predictions at baseline, yet under 50% occlusion its accuracy fell to 0.520 while mean confidence on incorrect predictions rose to 0.989.
It assigned 92.9% of probabilities below 0.01 or above 0.99.
Thus, favourable confidence behaviour on intact images did not carry over to these altered inputs.
A review strategy that flags only low-confidence predictions could miss high-confidence errors of this type, although no clinical triage rule or threshold was evaluated here.
Expected calibration error increased from 0.094 on intact images to 0.478 under occlusion.
Evaluating confidence together with discrimination under the same perturbation therefore revealed information that either baseline calibration or perturbed AUC alone would miss.
Probe angulation, acoustic coupling and field of view vary in clinical imaging, but constant masks do not reproduce these changes.

The observed discrimination-confidence mismatch motivates testing whether confidence remains informative under realistic acquisition variation; it does not demonstrate that the same failure occurs clinically.
Attribution adds a third dimension to this evaluation, but did not provide a stable anatomical account of the observed model differences.
The direction and magnitude of Grad-CAM metrics varied across seeds and methods.
For EfficientNet-B0, the small observed insertion advantage over random masking was not detected as significant in the original image-level test.
That result is inconclusive about equivalence and does not prove that.
the maps contain no relevant information.
Instead, seed and method variation, together with the limited insertion evidence, constrain what can be inferred from a plausible single-run map.
Reproducibility and faithfulness address different aspects of attribution and should not be inferred from visual plausibility alone.

Benchmarking studies elsewhere in medical imaging have reported that saliency maps localize abnormalities less accurately than expert readers [43] and can fail model-randomization and repeatability checks [44].

The held-out test subjects were separate from these training/validation partitions, but seed replication does not remove single-fold model-selection bias.
All images were acquired by one operator.
This reduces between-operator variation within the dataset but limits generalizability and may allow operator-specific features to influence classification.
The measured acquisitionparameter comparisons did not establish the absence of confounding.
Finally, the upper-to-lower activation ratio was introduced to separate spatial from amplitude-related differences in attention.
Because it was not reproducible here, we offer it as a diagnostic template whose outputs must themselves be checked for stability before anatomical interpretation.
The relevance to dentomaxillofacial imaging lies in comparing models and interpreting their outputs before considering diagnostic or procedural use.
Similar discrimination on intact images may coexist with different sensitivity to altered inputs, and a model may remain highly confident as discrimination deteriorates.
An attribution overlay provides further evidence only to the extent that its patterns are reproducible and supported by the evaluation used.
The present subregion-classification task demonstrates these evaluation issues within a limited intraoral ultrasound setting.

A useful evaluation would report discrimination and confidence together on both intact and clinically motivated altered inputs, then examine attribution reproducibility across training runs and methods and its performance against appropriate controls.
Such reporting could distinguish loss of discrimination accompanied by uncertainty from loss accompanied by confident errors, while making the limits of attribution-based interpretation explicit.
Stored checkpoints allow some of these checks without retraining, although realistic acquisition perturbations and independent validation require additional work.
These checks complement clinical validation and do not establish safety by themselves.
The present findings apply to the sampled buccal subregion task, evaluated training pipelines and specified masks.
Their value is in exposing differences between dimensions of model behaviour that would be obscured by a comparison based only on baseline discrimination.
The dataset comprises 477 images from 40 subjects at one institution, with only eight subjects in the held-out test set.

The subject-cluster bootstrap addresses within-subject dependence for the saved follow-up predictions but remains imprecise with so few clusters and conditions on the observed training data and fixed models.
Seed replication does not add independent participants.
Earlier image-level intervals and tests are exploratory and may be anticonservative.
Generalization beyond this cohort requires evaluation with additional centres and operators.
Expert re-classification supported agreement with acquisition-position labels in selected images, not pixel-level correspondence between attribution and anatomy.
Anatomical regions were not delineated.
Direct comparison against expert regions, alternative perturbation methods and model-randomization controls could provide additional evidence in future work.
Constant-intensity masks are artificial inputs.
Their effects may reflect loss of distributed information, distribution shift or both.
Geometric boundaries do not isolate individual tissue layers.
Differences between original and follow-up EfficientNet-B0 occluded AUCs also remain unexplained; changing batch size and environment are possible contributors, not demonstrated causes.
Repeatability of baseline and upper-mask predictions within one environment does not resolve this between-execution discrepancy.

Finally, this study addressed binary subregion classification, not vessel detection, flap viability assessment or surgical risk stratification; its results are not evidence for surgical decision support.
The possible explanations in Section 4.3 remain hypotheses.
The confidence-based review implications in Section 4.4 were not evaluated as a clinical workflow.
Future work could evaluate clinically motivated acquisition changes and extend perturbation assessment to continuous anatomical measurements.
A lack of output change after occlusion would need to be interpreted alongside redundant information and distribution shift rather than treated as proof that the region was unused.
In intraoral ultrasound subregion classification, similar observed baseline discrimination concealed different responses to synthetic occlusion.
Across five training seeds, EfficientNet-B0 fell below AUC 0.60 in 49 of 50 boundary-sweep conditions, while its errors under 50% occlusion became highly confident.
Spatial attributions were not consistently reproduced across seeds or class-activation methods, limiting anatomical interpretation from a single map.
Joint reporting of perturbation sensitivity, confidence under perturbation and attribution reproducibility therefore characterized model behaviour beyond baseline discrimination.
